newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, investment banks sign Eurobond accord.
newsitem.headline: Israel, investment banks sign Eurobond accord.

text.p: Israel on Tuesday formalised its plan to raise $750 million in the European debt market, signing an agreement with seven international investment houses.
The first part of the three-year Euro Medium Term Note Programme (EMTN) calls for a $200 million to $250 million debut Eurobond, probably in November, officials said.
Terms of the offering have yet to be set but it is likely to be a mix of dollars and several European currencies.
"Israel is selling its economy and people are buying," Finance Minister Dan Meridor said at the signing ceremony.
"It is important for the economy that we find ourselves also on the European map," he added, noting that until now Israel had focused on the U.S. debt market.

Merrill Lynch International is the arranger for the EMTN while the remaining dealers are Daiwa Europe Ltd, Deutsche Bank AG of London, Goldman Sachs International, Morgan Stanley & Co International, Swiss Bank Corp and UBS Ltd.
Morgan Guaranty Trust Co of New York is the issuing and principal paying agent.

Israel's foray into Europe is part of an effort to broaden its sources for raising financing, in light of the expiration of the $10 billion U.S. loan guarantee programme in 1998. Next year Israel plans to test the Asian market as well.
Its first offering without guarantees was a Yankee bond last year, which was more than three times oversubscribed, noted Accountant General Shai Talmon.
The fate of the Eurbond offering was given a boost this week when Standard & Poor's and Moody's reaffirmed Israel's A minus and A3 credit rating, respectively.
"The reconfirmation of the ratings is a very strong statement," said Stephen Marquardt, managing director of investment banking at Merrill Lynch International.
He said the agencies commonly review sovereign ratings when a new government comes into power, as in the case of the Israel.
"The new government is perceived very well," Marquardt said, adding that Israel should not have a problem raising sufficient financing once the guarantees run out.

"There is significant international demand for Israeli paper. It can become a well-known issuer, opening the market to Israeli companies," he said. The government and Israeli companies have already done syndicated loans in Europe, where the pricing has improved, he added.
John Heimann, Merrill Lynch chairman of global financial institutions, said the Israeli economy was perceived as "very healthy", with enviable growth rates of over six percent in recent years.
While growth is expected to slow to about four percent a year, there was "no fear of a recession", he added.
He said the current account deficit in the balance of payments, expected to widen from last year's $4.1 billion, was not yet perceived as a major problem.
Heimann said countries often go through cycles in the short term that are "not necessarily symptomatic of a long-term problem".
